title: Benchmarking LLM-as-a-Judge for Long-Form Output Evaluation (LongJudgeBench)

key_points.claim: Existing LLM-as-a-judge meta-evaluation benchmarks mostly use short outputs (a few hundred tokens), so there is little evidence on how reliable judges are for long-form outputs such as deep research reports.
key_points.evidence_quote: most prior benchmarks are built around candidate outputs of only a few hundred tokens, leaving limited evidence about judge reliability in long-form evaluation.

key_points.claim: The difficulty of long-form evaluation is not just length. It involves document-level demands such as organization, consistency across sections, and coverage.
key_points.evidence_quote: long-form evaluation involves qualitatively different document-level evaluation demands, such as assessing overall organization, cross-section consistency, and coverage and depth across multiple subtopics.

key_points.claim: LongJudgeBench covers five scenarios (including deep research) across six datasets. Candidate outputs average about 9,250 tokens, and all reference judgments come from experts.
key_points.evidence_quote: It provides candidate outputs averaging 9,249.7 tokens, together with task-specific evaluation protocols and expert reference judgments.

key_points.claim: The authors built a new deep-research dataset, RealDeepResearch: 640 documents in Chinese and English, kept in their original DOCX format and annotated by experts for about USD 2,260.
key_points.evidence_quote: RealDeepResearch, which contains 40 research tasks, 4 prompt styles, and 4 generation models, resulting in 640 long documents. RealDeepResearch covers both Chinese and English documents and preserves the original DOCX format

key_points.claim: The paper argues against using LLM-generated gold labels to meta-evaluate judges, because this risks circularity. That is its criticism of the concurrent Long-form RewardBench.
key_points.evidence_quote: most of its gold labels are produced by an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline rather than expert annotation, potentially causing circularity and judge-specific biases.

key_points.claim: Method: judge reliability is measured as agreement with expert judgments, using accuracy (the main metric), Spearman, and Kendall's tau-b, each computed per query group. Pairwise comparisons are run in both answer orders to reduce position bias.
key_points.evidence_quote: To reduce position bias in pairwise evaluation, we evaluate each pair in both answer orders and average the two results.

key_points.claim: Current judges are only moderately reliable. The best configuration (Qwen3-Max + reference) reaches 0.6721 accuracy, and the mean across all 32 model-setting combinations is 0.5627, barely above the 0.5 random baseline.
key_points.evidence_quote: Across all 32 model–setting combinations, only 12 exceed 0.60, and the overall mean is 0.5627, only slightly above the random pairwise baseline of 0.5.

key_points.claim: Being a stronger general-purpose model does not guarantee being a better judge: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5.2 scored lower than Qwen3-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.1.
key_points.evidence_quote: This suggests that stronger general-purpose capabilities may not always translate into stronger long-form judging performance.

key_points.claim: Realistic deep research reports (RealDR, with document structure and multilingual content) were among the hardest to judge, at 0.4393 accuracy versus 0.6454 on plain-text DR-Bench.
key_points.evidence_quote: RealDR reaches 0.4393, possibly reflecting the added difficulty of realistic document structure and multilingual content

key_points.claim: Giving the judge references improved average accuracy from 0.5313 to 0.5843. The gain was largest on verification tasks. Rubrics helped with multidimensional research-report evaluation, raising DR-Bench accuracy from 0.5454 to 0.7075.
key_points.evidence_quote: Among the four judging settings, Reference achieves the best average performance, improving the overall score from 0.5313 under Vanilla to 0.5843.

key_points.claim: The benefits of rubrics and references are not universal or additive: using both scored 0.5784, slightly below reference alone, and rubrics hurt accuracy on some tasks.
key_points.evidence_quote: the benefit of combining reference and rubric guidance is not simply additive: Ref.+Rubric reaches 0.5784, slightly below Reference alone at 0.5843.

key_points.claim: Turning on thinking mode for the judge (Qwen3-32B) lowered its overall average.
key_points.evidence_quote: the overall average, which decreases from 0.5745 without thinking to 0.5241 with thinking.

key_points.claim: The effect of output length depends on the dataset; it is not simply that longer outputs are judged worse.
key_points.evidence_quote: the relationship between output length and judge accuracy is dataset-specific and cannot be simply summarized as longer is worse.

key_points.claim: Failure mode: judges reward surface-level coverage. In one example, a 12K-token response that barely addressed the core question received 9.26 from the judge versus 5.87 from humans.
key_points.evidence_quote: This case shows that LLM judges can mistake surface richness for substantive answers.

key_points.claim: Failure mode: judges confuse domain concepts and perform poorly in specialized domains such as medical systematic reviews.
key_points.evidence_quote: The Qwen3-Max judge incorrectly treats Messages API streaming and Streamable HTTP as the same concept, assigning an overall score of 8.85, while the human score is only 5.37.

key_points.claim: Position bias is severe for some models. Swapping the order of the two candidates gave inconsistency rates from 10.6% up to 78.7% (GPT-4o-mini on WP-Bench).
key_points.evidence_quote: GPT-4o-mini shows an especially high inconsistency rate of 78.7% on WP-Bench, suggesting strong dependence on candidate order.

key_points.claim: Some judgments fail outright because of context-window overflow (when outputs, references and rubrics are combined) or safety refusals. These failures are counted as incorrect.
key_points.evidence_quote: Context-window overflow occurs when long prompts exceed the model’s input limit, especially when outputs, references, and rubrics are combined.

key_points.claim: The paper did not test more advanced judge designs such as retrieval-augmented, multi-agent, or calibration-based judging; the authors leave these to future work.
key_points.evidence_quote: more advanced judge designs, such as retrieval-augmented judging, multi-agent judging, and calibration-based methods, remain to be explored.

reliability_notes: This is a v1 arXiv preprint that has not been peer reviewed. The code link is anonymized, which suggests it is under review. It evaluates LLM judges for long-form outputs, including deep research reports, rather than research agents end to end, so it bears on only the output-evaluation part of the task. Temperature was set to 0 and one prompt setup was used per configuration. Failed judgments were counted as incorrect, which pushes some scores down. Some model names (GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi-K2.6) are recent, and the results are specific to those versions. The page fetched cleanly.
